parent: Thirty Madison (sister brands Cove, Facet, Nurx; care by KMG Medical Group)
model: US men's telehealth subscription for male pattern hair loss: a short marketing quiz names a compounded prescription product, the patient pays, and a licensed provider reviews a medical intake afterwards.

access.accountWall: Main and Gel funnels: /express/checkout, reached from the plan page button 'Continue to checkout' (one page asking name, address, phone, date of birth, email and card). Legacy quiz: /quiz/lead (name, email, phone) straight after the last question. Request flow: /request/lead (name, email) on the first screen. The medical intake (/consultation/intake) redirects to sign-in.
blockers: The medical questionnaire is behind payment and sign-in; its schema (keeps/intake-consultation) is only requested by signed-in pages, so it was not read. No bot protection was met.
access.coverageNote: Stage 1 read all three quizzes in served JavaScript. Stage 2 replayed all three baselines and ran 41 one-change experiments (19 main quiz, 3 gel, 19 legacy) to the plan page or account wall. Every product-changing rule read in the code was confirmed live. Not tested: the remaining 'no effect' options of the main quiz one by one (code shows no branch condition, 13 replays agreed), most of the 51 accepted states, the medical intake after payment and sign-in, and the clinician's decision. Keeps does not treat women (refers to Nurx).

engineSummary: Before payment the main Keeps quiz is a two-answer lookup, now proved live. 'How would you like to treat your hair loss?' picks the family (Topical Drop gives Drop/Drop+, anything else gives Chew/Chew+) and 'What's your top priority?' picks the strength ('simple & affordable' gives the finasteride product, anything else the dutasteride 'plus' product). Thirteen other one-change replays (onset under 6 months, advanced loss, patchy loss, earlier side effects, goal, state) changed nothing but the echoed label. The only stops are a 'Mostly Scalp' picture, twelve refused states and an unticked '18+ and assigned male at birth' box; women are referred to Nurx. The Gel funnel always names Gel+. The older /quiz is a real rule table, also proved live: location and pill preference choose finasteride, foam or oral minoxidil; tretinoin or vitamins swap foam for a compounded spray; dandruff, ketoconazole, saw palmetto, hair care and pomade each add one product; patchy loss goes to a clinician request. In every flow the medical screening happens after the account wall and payment.
strengths: Very short path: about ten taps and no typing to reach a named product and a price.
Patients steer the offer with two plain choices (oral or topical; strongest or cheapest), and switch links on the plan page show the other family at once.
An honest early stop for advanced baldness ('Mostly Scalp'): it tells the patient prescription treatment is unlikely to work and points to restoration or cosmetic options.
Clear price ladder with a large first-order discount and a 180-day money-back guarantee on the new compounded range.
Wide range: licensed generics (finasteride, minoxidil, ketoconazole), compounded combinations (oral and topical, finasteride or dutasteride) and cosmetic add-ons.
Honest legal labelling on product pages: compounded products are marked 'not FDA-approved'.
weaknesses: 'You're approved' and 'clinically recommended' are shown before any medical question; the loaders ('Confirming clinical eligibility') are timed animations.
Proved live: 'Had side effects' from earlier treatment, onset under 6 months and patchy loss change nothing, give no warning and ask no follow-up (runs/exp-08, 11, 12).
The default for every man who does not ask for cheap is a compounded dutasteride product (off-label for hair loss in the US), never licensed finasteride first.
Payment is taken before the medical intake; a product page says 'You won't be charged until your prescription is approved' while the checkout says the card is charged and refunded if not approved.
Age and sex are checked with one tick box; no women's service at all (referred to Nurx).
Renewal price ($204.99 per 3 months for Chew+) is about double the first order ($100) and appears only in the checkout small print.
Two older funnels (legacy /quiz and /plan-selection) still run with different logic and products, so the same man can be sent to different treatments depending on the entry page.
opportunities: Ask the real safety questions before payment (heart, blood pressure, fertility plans, mood, earlier side effects) and let them visibly steer the offer, then say 'likely suitable, a clinician will confirm' instead of 'approved'.
Start with licensed finasteride and step up to dutasteride only on a reason (no response, intolerance) and say why.
Triage patchy, sudden or recent loss and scalp symptoms (redness, burning, scaling) to a clinician instead of passing them silently.
Serve women: Keeps sends them away; a combined men-and-women service with a proper female pathway (pregnancy, contraception, PCOS) is an open gap.
Show the renewal price next to the first-order price.
